awd_titl_txt: Conference: Center for Aerosol Science and Technology (CAST) Workshop on Wildland Fire Emissions and Indoor Air Quality
awd_abstract_narration:
This NSF award provides travel and organization support for the Center for Aerosol Science and Technology (CAST) Workshop held at the University of Miami in 2025. The hybrid workshop will gather researchers and students to address indoor air quality issues resulting from wildland fire emissions. The research will have a particular focus on the Southeast U.S., which experiences more wildland fires than any other region of the U.S. The workshop will feature keynote speeches and panel discussions by national experts, as well as tutorials, hands-on instrument demonstrations, and student competitions to facilitate knowledge transfer and develop communication skills. Results will be disseminated through a publication summarizing the current state of knowledge and potential solutions. Society will benefit from this workshop through the advancement of knowledge on wildland fire emissions. Such information can be used to develop new systems to address indoor air pollution and associated human health impacts caused by these fires. 
 
The University of Miami Center for Aerosol Science and Technology (CAST) workshop focuses on advanced indoor air quality control and impacts of wildland fire emissions in the Southeast U.S. Wildland fires are a growing global concern, particularly in the Southeast U.S., which experiences the largest number of wildland fires, comparable to the rest of the U.S. combined. Significant gaps in our understanding exist on how pollutants from wildland fires impact both climate and the infiltration of air pollutants to indoor environments. Such infiltration exacerbates human health risks due to poor ventilation and filtration. To address these challenges, the CAST workshop will present new research findings on Southeast U.S. biomass burning emissions, advanced air quality sensor design, risk assessment methods, and building controls to mitigate health risks associated with indoor air pollution. Hands-on instrumentation and tutorial sessions will demonstrate state-of-the-art technology for monitoring and controlling air pollutants, equipping attendees with the skills needed to tackle these research problems. The involvement of non-profit organizations, such as Healthy Little Havana, will enhance community engagement on these issues. Additionally, student participation will foster career development and contribute to a skilled future STEM workforce. Results will be disseminated through a published manuscript that summarizes our current understanding and potential solutions to issues associated with wildland fire emissions and indoor air quality control. Additional benefits to society result from supporting the inclusion of attendees from diverse backgrounds to broaden participation in the fields of air quality and environmental engineering and science.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF grant made it possible to organize and deliver the 4th Annual Workshop on Aerosol Science and Technology at the University of Miami on January 15 to 16, 2026. The workshop brought together students, researchers, public-health experts, community representatives, and industry participants to advance education and collaboration in aerosol science and technology. The workshop delivered sessions with a focus on wildland fire emissions (including emission characterization and impacts on air quality and environment) and indoor air quality (including pollutant characterization, physical, chemical, and biological transformation, and control technologies). 

The intellectual merit of the project was addressed by creating a multidisciplinary forum focused on the science, measurement, and impacts of aerosols. Aerosols are tiny particles suspended in air that can affect air quality, human health, climate, weather, visibility, and industrial processes. The workshop covered several important and emerging topics, including portable and wearable air sensors, emerging air pollutants, climate impacts of atmospheric aerosols, fire emissions and public health, coastal aerosols, nanoparticle technology, and advanced materials characterization. Through three tutorials, four technical sessions and panel discussions, and 25 poster presentations, participants exchanged current knowledge on how aerosols are generated, measured, transformed in the environment, and connected to health and climate outcomes. 

A major outcome of the workshop was the integration of classroom-style instruction with hands-on learning. 98 participants from 30 institutions attended three tutorial lectures from leading experts and then engaged with state-of-the-art particle measurement and characterization instruments through demonstrations by seven instrument vendors. This format helped bridge fundamental aerosol science with practical measurement approaches used in research, industry, and environmental monitoring. The workshop also provided opportunities for participants to learn about emerging research challenges, such as smoke exposure from fires, the role of aerosols in coastal environments, the detection of emerging air pollutants, and the use of sensor technologies for air-quality monitoring. 

The broader impacts of the project were addressed through workforce development, student training, professional networking, and engagement across disciplines. Through the support of this NSF grant, students and early-career researchers attended the workshop, presented posters, interacted with senior scientists, and participated in networking activities with academic, public-health, community, and industry partners. Poster awards recognized student contributions and encouraged continued participation in aerosol science and engineering. The workshop also strengthened connections between university researchers and external stakeholders, including public-health leaders, community organizations, and companies developing aerosol measurement technologies. 

Overall, the project strengthened the Center for Aerosol Science and Technology as a regional and national platform for aerosol education, interdisciplinary research exchange, and professional development. By connecting aerosol science with public health, climate, environmental monitoring, coastal environments, and advanced technologies, the workshop helped broaden participation in aerosol research and supported the development of the next generation of scientists and engineers working on air quality and environmental challenges.
